The **idea** is to build a performance metric which will be used to compare everyone's models when these will be completed. We agreed that our models will output the final ranking of teams of the Premier League season we will be predicting.

## Performance metric

Our **idea** is to build a performance metric which will add weights as:

| Actual, $a_i$ | Prediction, $p_i$ | Weight, $w_i$ |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Top 5 | Correct position | 1 |
| Top 5 | Incorrect position but within top 5 | $w_i = \frac{\vert P_5 \cap A_5\vert}{5}$ |
| Top 5 | Predicted outside top 5 | $f(x_i) = -(1-\exp^{-x_i})$ |
| Outside top 5 (excluding bottom 3) | Correct position | 0.5 |
| Outside top 5 (excluding bottom 3) | Incorrectly predicted in top 5 | $f(x_i) = -(1-\exp^{-x_i})$ |
| Outside top 5 (excluding bottom 3) | Incorrect position outside top 5 | $f(x_i) = -(1-\exp^{-0.1x_i})$ |
| Bottom 3 | Correctly predicted within bottom 3 | 1 |
| Bottom 3 | Predicted outside bottom 3 | $f(x_i) = -(1-\exp^{-0.1x_i})$ |

The reason why we add greater weight to the first 5 observations is because, we assume that the teams that fall into the first 5 positions at the end of the league will pass to the next championship (so focusing on this will also help us have an idea on how to continue the prediction).

Note: The reason why we are dividing the distance by 19 for an incorrect prediction outside of top 5 is because $\text{max}\{a_i,p_i\} = 19$ and similarly for an incorrect prediction outside top 5 we have $\text{max}\{a_i,p_i\} = 14$.

Notes:

1)  We aim to keep $w_i \in [-1,1]$.

2)  We care about the top 5 teams the most since these will then enter the Champions League so $w_i = 1$ (money won)

3)  We care about the bottom 3 as these will get relegates for the next season so $w_i = 1$ (money lost)

4)  Actual and predicted teams aren't in the same position but are within the first 5 so $w_i = \frac{\vert P_5 \cap A_5\vert}{5}$ where $P_5$ is the set of teams that are in the predicted top 5, and $A_5$ is the set of teams in the actual top 5.

5)  predicted takes values in position 8+ while actual takes position within first 5 so $f(x_i) = -(1-\exp^{-kx_i})$ where $x_i=d(a_i,p_i)$ and k =1.

6)  actual is outside of top 5:

- predicted = actual $w_i = 0.5$ (not losing or winning money ish)
- We care about the bottom 3 as these will get relegates for the next season so $w_i = 1$ (money lost)
- else $f(x_i) = -(1-\exp^{-kx_i})$ where $x_i=d(a_i,p_i)$ and k = ??

Here is the code for the total weight we give to our model: range is [-16,14] (??)

```{r}
pm <- function(predicted, actual) {
  
  n <- length(actual)
  # Identify the top five teams
  P5 <- which(predicted <= 5)
  A5 <- which(actual <= 5)

  # Calculate overlap between predicted and actual top five
  overlap <- length(intersect(P5, A5)) / 5

  # Identify bottom three positions
  bottom3 <- (n - 2):n

  wt <- numeric(n)

  for (i in 1:n) {

    p <- predicted[i]
    a <- actual[i]

    d <- abs(p - a)

    if (a <= 5) { # Actual position is in the top five
      
      if (p == a) {
        w <- 1

      } else if (p <= 5) {
        w <- overlap

      } else {
        w <- -(1 - exp(-d))
      }

    } else {# Actual position is outside the top five

      if (a %in% bottom3) {# Actual team is in the bottom three

        if (p %in% bottom3) {
          w <- 1

        } else {
          w <- -(1 - exp(-d))
        }

      } else if (p <= 5) {# Incorrectly predicted in the top five
        
        w <- -(1 - exp(-d))

      } else if (p == a) {# Correctly predicted outside the top five

        w <- 0.5

      } else {# Incorrectly predicted outside the top five
        k <- 0.1
        w <- -(1 - exp(-k * d))
      }
    }

    wt[i] <- w
  }

  return(sum(wt))
}

pm_adjusted <- function(predicted, actual, historical_features, season_features, total_features, lambda_H = 1, lambda_S = 2) {

  original_pm <- pm(predicted, actual)

  penalty_H <- lambda_H *(historical_features / total_features)

  penalty_S <- lambda_S *(season_features / total_features)

  adjusted_pm <- original_pm - penalty_H - penalty_S

  return(adjusted_pm)
}

pm_adjusted <- function(predicted, actual, historical_features, season_features, total_features, lambda_S) {

  original_pm <- pm(predicted, actual)

  penalty_H <- historical_features / 22

  penalty_S <- lambda_S *(season_features / 22)

  adjusted_pm <- original_pm - penalty_H - penalty_S

  return(adjusted_pm)
}
```

## Spearman's rank correlation coefficient

### Intuition

Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, $\rho$, is a number ranging from −1 to 1 that indicates how strongly two sets of ranks are correlated (in our case `predicted` vs `actual`). It is a nonparametric measure of rank correlation. It assesses how well the relationship between two variables (`predicted` and `actual`) can be described using a monotonic function (i.e. \$f(x_i) \leq f(x\_{i+1}) \$ or \$f(x_i) \geq f(x\_{i+1}) \$). It is used in situations where the ranking of a dataset is important, for instance in sports.

A perfect Spearman correlation of +1 or −1 occurs when each of the variables is a perfect monotone function of the other.

(eg. $f($`actual[i]`$) = f($`predicted[i]`$) \leq f($`actual[i+1]`$) = f($`predicted[i+1]`$)$ eg.`predicted` = (3,2,4,1) and `actual` = (1,2,3,4)).

Intuitively, the Spearman correlation between two variables will be high when observations have a similar (or equal with correlation = 1) rank between the two variables, and low when observations have a dissimilar(or fully opposed with correlation = -1) rank between the two variables.

### Formula

For a sample size $n$, the $n$ pairs of raw scores $(X_i,Y_i)$ are converted to ranks $(\text{R}[X_i],\text{R}[Y_i])$ and the Spearman rank correlation, $\rho$, is calculated as $$\rho [ \text{R}[X] \ ,\text{R}[Y] \ ] = \frac{\text{cov}[ \text{R}[X] \ ,\text{R}[Y]]}{\sigma_{\text{R}[X]}\sigma_{\text{R[Y]}}}, $$ where:

- $\text{cov}[ \text{R}[X] \ ,\text{R}[Y]]$ is the covariance of the rank variables,

- $\sigma_{\text{R}[X]}$ and $\sigma_{\text{R[Y]}}$ are the standard deviations of the rank variables.

### Conclusion

This tells us how well our model predicted the rank of teams at the end of the season. However, to compare different models this might not be ideal since it doesn't consider the complexity of the model. I can use this method instead to test how well my model performs when predicting the rank.

```{r}
pm <- function(predicted, actual) {
  wt <- c()

  for (i in 1:length(predicted)) {
    p <- predicted[i]  # predicted position
    a <- actual[i]     # actual position
    d <- abs(p - a)    # distance between predicted and actual i.e. residual

    if (a <= 5) {  # team actually finished in the top five

      if (p == a) { # actual and predicted teams are in the same position within the first 5
        w <- 1 
      } else if (p <= 5) { # actual and predicted teams aren't in the same position but are within the first 5
        w <- 0.7 
      } else { # predicted takes values in position 6+ while actual takes position within first 5
        w <- -(d^2 / 19) # max_i(d_i) = 19
      }

    } else {  # team actually finished outside the top five

      if (p <= 5) { # incorrectly predicted in the top five
        w <- 0  
      } else if (p == a) { # correctly predicted outside of top 5
        w <- 0.4
      } else { # incorrectly predicted outside of top 5 actual outside of top 5 and predicted also outside but not equal
        w <- -(d / 14) # notice for one space wrong w = -0.07, for 14 spaces wrong (max distance) w = -1
      }
    }

    wt <- c(wt, w)
  }

  sum(wt) 
}
#check what's the maximum and minimum score
pm(predicted = actual_table$Position, actual = actual_table$Position)
pm(predicted = 21-actual_table$Position, actual = actual_table$Position)
```
